problem: The authors' earlier object-centric topological macro-action DQN navigator relied on the simulator's ground-truth pose and detections. Full SLAM is heavy and fragile in simulation, and it is more than a topological controller needs.
motivation: A real robot must estimate its own pose from noisy sensors, but mammal navigation suggests that locally consistent, approximate metric information plus a topological structure is enough. The paper tests whether a drifting, globally inconsistent pose estimate still supports macro-action navigation in large photorealistic apartments.
key_idea: Replace the ground-truth pose with a lightweight object-centric localizer (per-object ORB anchors, Kabsch alignment, EKF with a motion model) that drifts jointly with nearby objects. Combine it with visual homing so that local consistency suffices for topological macro-action navigation.
insight: Local consistency is enough because macro actions follow short graph edges and visual homing takes over near the target, so global drift of meters does not stop the agent from reaching targets. The No-EKF ablation shows the heading error grows to 80-104 degrees without the motion model, and Motion-Only shows the position drifts to 3-4 m without the Kabsch measurement, so the two parts do separate jobs. Conventional success is inflated by chance give-up Found declarations, so the paper adds a 'genuine success' metric, which separates the trained DQN from Random-Macro (e.g. 85.4% vs 54.1% at one target).
method: Decision layer: DRRN-style DQN inherited from prior work, scoring each known object node (image patches x one-hot task progress via outer product) as a macro action, with Boltzmann exploration.

Topological map: undirected weighted graph of backbone nodes (visited estimated poses, waypoints) and object nodes (id, 3D position, patches). Object positions are written once and never updated, so the map is not globally consistent.
ORB object landmark bank: ORB keypoints are detected only inside each object's semantic mask and stored with 3D anchors back-projected from depth. Only re-found anchors are used for localization.

Kabsch pose measurement: SE(2) alignment of matched observed points and stored anchors, using inverse-distance weights and SVD. It gives a position and yaw measurement plus residuals used as a trust signal.

EKF: SE(2) state (x,z,yaw) with motion-model prediction for forward and turn actions under injected actuation noise (1° turn, 0.01 m forward, 0.005 m slip). Kabsch measurements are fused with noise scaled by residuals, and inconsistent measurements are rejected.
Map-write gate: objects are added to the map only when the pose looks reliable (number of matches, EKF uncertainty); otherwise the write is deferred.

Controller: shortest path over the graph to a backbone node near the target, then visual homing from the semantic mask and depth (turn toward target, step forward, signal Found), with stall fallbacks.

setting.backbone: DQN (DRRN-style, conv feature extractor + FC) trained with RL; classical ORB/Kabsch/EKF localizer; hand-built controller
setting.training_data: RL in Habitat multi-room apartments, five seeds per condition and task type; immediate and terminal reward; no external data
setting.observation: RGB-D with simulator-provided semantic masks and object ids; no GPS/compass
setting.action_space: macro actions (navigate to a known object node) executed as low-level forward/turn-left/turn-right plus Found
setting.privileged: Simulator-provided object semantic masks and ids (no object detection); GT pose only in the GT-Pose oracle condition

numbers_note: Custom Habitat multi-object task, not a standard benchmark. The split label 'val' is a placeholder since the paper does not name a split. Only the Full system, plus the 1-target oracle for reference, is listed; the other conditions are in Table 1. Success rates are in Table 1 and Fig. 2.
results: With noisy actuation and no GT pose, the Full system reaches 92.7% conventional / 85.4% genuine success at one target, and 57.3-59.2% (27.0-30.3% genuine) at three targets. Position drift stays at a few meters and yaw error at 13-39 degrees. It leads the noisy-pose ablations on the genuine measure in most cells and beats Random-Macro clearly on genuine success at one target (85.4% vs 54.1%), but stays below the GT-Pose oracle (96.9% genuine at one target, 100% conventional).
limitations: ORB feature extraction inside every object mask is computationally costly.
Object masks and ids come from the simulator, so real object detection and its noise are not addressed.

Much of the reliability rests on a hand-engineered controller (Random-Macro still reaches many targets), and a gap to the GT-Pose oracle remains and widens with sequence length; the Full system is not consistently better than the ablations on terminal-reward tasks.
